title: The right entanglement for perfect nonlocality and zero-error communication
abstract: We identify a structural mechanism by which perfect play in a nonlocal game requires and self-tests a specific non-maximally entangled state. To this end, we construct a Flagged Magic-Square game by extending the standard Magic-Square game with an additional ``flag'' outcome and two additional questions for each player. The game admits a perfect strategy using a state with Schmidt coefficients proportional to $(1,\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2})$. We give a direct algebraic proof that maximally entangled strategies have winning probability bounded away from one, independently of dimension. Moreover, the game self-tests this state, providing an example of a two-party pseudo-telepathy game that certifies a specific non-maximally entangled state. Our construction illustrates how adding suitable constraints to a rigid measurement geometry can enforce specific Schmidt ratios and provides a modular route to further self-tests based on other rigid pseudo-telepathy games.   We establish a general game-to-channel reduction that transfers separations in the game model to one-shot zero-error communication over classical channels. Applied to the Flagged Magic-Square game, it yields a classical channel for which entanglement permits the zero-error transmission of ten messages in a single use, whereas any finite-dimensional maximally entangled resource permits at most nine. Thus, maximally entangled states are not a universally optimal entanglement resource for zero-error communication over classical noisy channels.
summary: This paper establishes a deep connection between perfect strategies in nonlocal quantum games and the capacity of entanglement-assisted zero-error communication channels. By analyzing the Flagged Magic-Square game, the authors show that optimal performance requires a specific non-maximally entangled state, proving that maximal entanglement is not always the best resource for quantum information tasks.
main_problem: The paper investigates the relationship between achieving perfect play in specific nonlocal quantum games and the fundamental limits of zero-error quantum communication.
main_result: It proves that for certain games, the optimal entanglement resource required for perfect play is a specific non-maximally entangled state, demonstrating that maximally entangled states are not universally optimal for zero-error communication.
method: The authors employ a general game-to-channel reduction, linking game separations to zero-error codes, and use algebraic proofs involving structural constraints on quantum measurements.
model_or_system: The primary model is the Flagged Magic-Square game (GFMS), a two-party pseudo-telepathy game. The quantum resource is a bipartite pure entangled state, and the communication channel is a one-shot classical channel assisted by entanglement.
key_observables: Schmidt coefficients (e.g., proportional to $(1, \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2})$), winning probabilities ($\omega^*$, $\omega_{ME}$), and the number of messages transmitted with zero error.
important_parameters: The dimension of the Hilbert spaces, the overlap constant $c$, and the number of messages (e.g., 10 vs 9).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the existence of a general game-to-channel reduction and the ability to derive constraints from the structure of the game's measurement outcomes.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the encoding/decoding process for one-shot entanglement-assisted zero-error communication.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the game model and establishes the game-to-channel reduction. It then uses algebraic techniques to analyze the constraints imposed by perfect play, leading to the characterization of the required non-maximally entangled state and its implications for communication capacity.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, game-theoretic framework to test the optimality of entanglement resources, which is crucial for understanding fundamental limits in quantum communication protocols.
